title: And Now Ladies and Gentlement
full_review:
A jewel thief and a nightclub singer meet under curious circumstances in the unusual drama "And Now Ladies and Gentlemen" (Paramount Classics).

Jeremy Irons never seems to take on a straightforward, ordinary character. His characters always seem to reside in the gray area of life. It is no different with his latest protagonist, Valentin Valentin (so named because of his birth on St. Valentine's Day). Englishman Valentin is a jewel thief and master of disguise who has managed to pull off heists from Bulgari and other haute-bauble shops using humorous bluff and charming deceit. But now he is being nagged by a secret wish: to start anew, and possibly even to reimburse those from whom he has stolen. He begins by setting sail on a luxury yacht, seeking solace in the deep blue sea.

Meanwhile, jazz chanteuse Jane Lester (recording artist Patricia Kaas) is nursing a broken heart, thanks to a philandering trumpet player. Her heartbreak leads her to Morocco, where she takes a gig singing in a grand Fez hotel, and where Valentin's boat has crashed. But what draws them together are these strange symptoms they both have been experiencing. At various times, Jane and Valentin suffer from blackouts and severe memory lapses. She has been forgetting the lyrics to the song she's singing and he can't remember where he has stashed the stolen merchandise, or whether he has stolen at all. They "meet cute" awaiting their individual CAT-scans.

Within the story is another layer, where director Claude Lelouch plays with the sequence of events and punctuates reality with the characters' dreams. As Jane is experiencing one of her "moments," she is seen fading from full color to sepia then to black and white, until the moment passes and she returns to full color. Lelouch has also rolled light-hearted moments into this downbeat love story, mostly associated with Valentin's disguises and trickery when he robs. Yet, Lelouch has difficulty maintaining an even tone throughout the film. It seems he wants to imitate the various ups and downs of life, but the result is not as good as the intent. And as the film moves leisurely on, the script becomes increasingly muddled and loses momentum.

Although Valentin's desire to make amends for his wayward ways is commendable, the film's tenor can make his thievery seem "cool." In a twisted way, the film seems to indicate that his brain tumor is his punishment. But even this seems tenuous.

Strange, visually intense and with some parts better than others, "And Now Ladies and Gentlemen" is a mixed bag, leaving the viewer reflecting yet vaguely dissatisfied.

Subtitles.

Due to affairs and romantic complications with a smattering of crass words and an instance of rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops' classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
